data.title: Democrats want 'Medicare for More.' Then comes the hard part
data.description:
Democrats are coalescing around a plan to expand Medicare coverage to more Americans when they take control of Congress in January, a consensus policy that could bridge a divide between the party’s liberal and moderate wings. 

Both sides agree that they want to pursue “Medicare for More” quickly next year. But as Democrats eye ways to quickly lower costs, internal divisions over whether to push for “Medicare for All” could complicate a longer-term agenda for healthcare reform. 

Last week, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), whom Democrats nominated to be Speaker next term, outlined a plan to lower the Medicare eligibility age from 65 to 55, cover children under 18 years old and expand Medicare coverage for dental, vision and hearing benefits.  

Jeffries also emphasized an immediate focus on reversing Medicaid cuts under the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and restoring the Affordable Care Act’s (ACA) temporary enhanced premium tax credits that expired at the end of last year.  

“Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” Jeffries said during a press conference Tuesday. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable.”  

In the past, Democrats have been split between those who support Medicare for All and those who prefer incremental changes that don’t eliminate private insurance.  

Buoyed by the victory of candidates like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D) in Michigan, progressives in the House and Senate are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.   

But at least for now, the factions appear united in moving toward a more middle ground.  

Lawmakers in the Congressional Progressive Caucus (CPC) welcomed what Jeffries outlined but emphasized they believe it’s only the first step in the broader march toward single-payer healthcare.  

Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), a CPC member, said he believes Jeffries’s immediate Medicare expansion plan is “very achievable.” 

“I think we have such a large majority that this step forward is going to be something that we’re going to be able to accomplish,” he said. “But our first step is undoing a lot of the Big Beautiful Bill stuff.” 

Frost noted that the incremental Medicare expansion proposal has also received support from Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), the longtime standard-bearer for Medicare for All who is expected to chair the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions next Congress. 

Sanders on Wednesday praised Jeffries’s Medicare expansion plan, dubbing it “the first year [of] Medicare for All.” 

“I think the word is getting out that it is no longer, from a political point of view, from a policy point of view, good enough to tinker around the edges,” Sanders said. “Yes, we have to protect those people who lost their Medicaid, ACA premiums — I’m all in on that. But I think increasingly the American people and elected officials understand the current healthcare system is broken.” 

Shortly after the elections, Sanders outlined his own plan to lower the Medicare eligibility age by 10 years, include vision and dental care in Medicare, and guarantee health insurance for all children through age 19.  

El-Sayed also jumped in this week to back the House leader’s proposal as a “great start.”  

The Michigan Democrat made instituting a single-payer healthcare system a key tenet of his Senate campaign.  

While major change is unlikely in the next two years with President Trump still in office, advocates are looking to set the agenda with an eye toward the 2028 presidential election.  

Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.), another CPC member, expressed uncertainty Thursday about the ability to get Trump’s signature on a Medicare expansion package.  

“I don’t know if we’re going to be able to do very much with Trump, but I do think that the first steps are really critical, and putting back funding to an infrastructure that has been starved is important too,” Grijalva said.  

The progressive lawmaker, who supports Medicare for All as a long-term goal, acknowledged the challenges associated with an immediate transition to a universal single-payer healthcare system.  

“Ideally, we want to get to Medicare for All relatively quickly, but I even heard Sen. Sanders say if we just flip a switch, you know, we could collapse a system that is already struggling,” she said. “So we don’t want to do that.” 

If the Medicare expansion idea gains traction in the next Congress, progressives will want to see real movement toward Medicare for All, something neither Jeffries nor Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) has endorsed. That would likely create internal tensions within the party as it looks ahead to the 2028 presidential election. 

But at the same time, letting a bill come to the floor during the Trump presidency would catapult Medicare for All directly into the 2028 conversation and show Democrats no longer fear attacks about taking away people’s private insurance.  

Rep. Ami Bera (D-Calif.), a physician and member of the centrist New Democrat Coalition, said a workable long-term plan will be contingent on factors like cost and coverage.  

Bera stressed a more immediate focus on reversing cuts made under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also known as H.R. 1.  

“Those aren’t the long-term solutions, but those at least give us time to lower costs for Americans, increase access, and then I think we can work on the longer-term ideas,” he said.  

As many adults and families struggle to afford health costs, the popularity of Medicare for All is growing. A KFF poll in September showed two-thirds of Americans favored a “single government plan.”    

A national debate would likely include more details about costs and trade-offs that aren’t being captured in surface-level campaign slogans.  

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin (D) praised Jeffries’s plan as a “very meaningful and substantive proposal” that could bridge divides within the Democratic Party over long-term healthcare goals.  

“It would undoubtedly win the support of a lot of people who want to move towards a national health system with Medicare for All, and I think it could gain a lot of support from other people who understand the huge gaps that exist,” Raskin said. “So I think that’s a shrewd proposal for him to advance.” 

Nathaniel Weixel contributed.

data.title: Virginia reports first measles-related death of 2026
data.description:
A young child in Virginia died after testing positive for measles, the state’s health department said Friday, marking the first death tied to the illness in the state this year.

The department said the child was aged 0-4 but declined to share further identifying information, such as vaccination status or other details related to the death, due to privacy concerns.

The fatal case in Virginia is the second reported measles-associated death since the Pan-American Health Organization announced this week it revoked the U.S.’s measles elimination status, declaring the disease endemic amid an ongoing outbreak.

In 2026, states have reported a total of 12 deaths tied to the disease, though the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s (CDC) currently count currently sits at six as of Friday night.

The discrepancies between these reported death tolls have become a source of contention between state officials and federal ones, specifically Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — who has sent mixed signals on the administration’s vaccine stance in recent months.

Virginia has recorded 220 measles cases so far this year, with just 1 percent in unvaccinated individuals, according to the commonwealth’s dashboard. More cases are concentrated in Charlotte County, a rural county in Southside Virginia, than anywhere else in the state.

Only a few patients have been hospitalized statewide, and the University of Virginia medical center revealed Monday it was treating a patient with measles — warning students to isolate if they develop symptoms and check their vaccination status.

But no state has been hit harder with the measles outbreak than Pennsylvania, which accounts for more than 25 percent of cases in the entire country and a majority of states’ reported deaths.

The CDC continues to say the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the most effective way to fight the infection, but just a few months ago, Trump signed an executive order recommending breaking up the MMR vaccine into three doses. The shot is typically given once at 12-15 months and again at 4-6 years.

At an event in the Oval Office in August, Trump suggested the combined shot was “lethal” without providing any evidence.

data.title: Democratic Sen.-elect Colom responds to Trump's praise
data.description:
Sen.-elect Scott Colom (D-Miss.) reacted in an interview Friday to President Trump’s recent praise of his midterm campaign strategy, saying his tactic of reaching out to Republicans during the election cycle shows how he plans to represent Mississippi.

Colom went viral on the campaign trail for a video he shared in which he tried to earn the support of voters in line for a Mississippi Trump rally. In an interview with sports commentator Stephen A. Smith last week, the president said he gave the Democrat “a lot of credit” for the move.

When asked in an interview with MS NOW about the president’s praise, Colom explained his decision to campaign on the other side of the aisle and said the strategy helped him identify cross-party priorities.

“I want to represent those people. So, it was my job to go listen to them, and I found out we had a lot in common,” Colom told anchor Ari Melber. “They were saying the same stuff I was hearing across the state: high gas, high groceries, get out of the war in Iran.”

Colom won an upset victory in a historically red state Trump claimed by more than 20 points in 2024, unseating GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. He was the first Democrat Mississippi elected to the Senate in over 40 years and will become the first Black lawmaker to hold the state’s seat since 1871.

He may be elected for a six-year term, but Colom has said he is continuing to bring his message to the other side. The senator-elect announced Thursday he would hold a town hall in Itawamba County, the place where he received the lowest share of the vote.

“Itawamba County is where I received my lowest percentage of the vote on Election Day. But I promised to be a senator for all Mississippi and I meant it,” Colom wrote in a post on Facebook. “No matter where you live or how you voted, your voice matters and I’ll always show up for you.”

The senator-elect said in Friday’s interview that campaigning to Republicans shows “the type of leader I’m gonna be.”

Some attributed Colom’s success in his Senate bid to his viral ads, including the clip of him speaking to voters at the Trump rally and the infamous “pick another protein” ad — where his campaign capitalized on a remark from Hyde-Smith about high beef prices.

Trump said in his interview with Smith the rally line at which Colom campaigned “went 10 miles long,” a claim the Democrat laughed off as an exaggeration in his Friday interview with MS NOW.

“Ten miles is crazy,” Colom said. “It was a long line, but it wasn’t ten miles.”

data.title: Former Jackson, Mississippi, mayor sentenced to federal prison for bribery
data.description:
The former mayor of Jackson, Miss., was sentenced to more than three years in federal prison after pleading guilty to bribery charges from his time in office.

Former Mayor Chokwe Antar Lumumba (D) was indicted on charges related to a bribery scheme he admitted to engaging in alongside former Hinds County District Attorney Jody Owens (D) and former Jackson City Council president Aaron Banks (D). Lumumba was sentenced Friday, the Associated Press reported, and Banks and Owens had already been sentenced to prison.

A 2024 indictment shows that Owens facilitated more than $80,000 in bribe payments to Lumumba and Banks in exchange for their votes to approve a multi-million–dollar real estate development in downtown Jackson. 

Owens in turn was receiving payments of over $100,000 from people he believed were real estate brokers, using his relationship with Lumumba and Banks to solicit the funds. The real estate brokers were actually undercover FBI agents.

Lumumba is the son of former Jackson Mayor Chokwe Lumumba, a civil rights attorney who served as mayor until his death in 2014. The younger Lumumba ran for office just a few years after his father’s death and became the youngest mayor in city history at just 34. 

He lost reelection in 2025 after the bribery charges became public, losing the Democratic primary runoff election to current Mayor John Horhn by nearly 50 points.

As mayor, he oversaw a city in a water crisis. Jackson’s water system failed in 2022, leaving more than 150,000 residents without safe drinking water for months.

data.title: Permitting reform bill clears major hurdle toward becoming law
data.description:
Presented by EQT
{beacon}

Energy & Environment

Energy & Environment

 

The Big Story 

Senate approves major permitting reform bill

The Senate passed a major bill Thursday seeking to speed up the build-out of the nation’s energy production and infrastructure — taking a massive step toward the legislation becoming law.

Greg Nash

The bill was passed by a vote of 62-33, with most of the Senate GOP’s support. Just two Republicans, Sens. Mike Rounds (S.D.) and Josh Hawley (Mo.), voted against the legislation.

 

While it was a bipartisan effort — spearheaded by Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) — Democratic support in the upper chamber was more limited. 

 

The bill, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), seeks to address long-standing complaints from various industries that infrastructure projects take too long to build in the U.S.

 

The legislation now heads to the House, where it’s also expected to have significant bipartisan support despite a split among Democrats. The White House is backing the bill, and it has issued a statement of support saying BAAJA “would remove major obstacles to building the infrastructure we need in this country.”

 

In the House, the Democratic caucus is divided on the bill. It appears to have significant GOP support — although at least one powerful Republican said he’d like to see some changes to the legislation.

 

The bill also contends with a crowded lame-duck calendar and absences. On Friday, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) called on his colleagues to show up and vote on issues including permitting reform.

 

“We’re getting very positive signals,” Capito told reporters when asked about the bill’s prospects in the House. She also noted supporters had spoken with several groups in the lower chamber but cautioned, “I would take nothing for granted.”

 

Some key provisions:

  • The bill aims to improve the nation’s ability to build power lines — a key step in getting renewable energy projects onto the grid — by allowing federal regulators to approve their construction if states don’t act.
  • It contains provisions that seek to prevent presidents from yanking existing permits from energy of all types — combating President Trump’s ability to block already approved wind projects and moves made by Democratic presidents, such as revoking approval from the Keystone XL pipeline.
  • BAAJA also exempts certain activities, including expansions to natural gas pipelines, from environmental reviews and limits those reviews to only alternatives that meet the goal of a project’s sponsor company.
  • It additionally restricts lawsuits against projects by mandating they be filed within 150 days of a proposal’s approval.
  • The bill also seeks to rein in increased electricity costs from large data centers, forcing them to pay for any costs stemming from their high electricity demand.

Read more at TheHill.com.

data.title: California man found guilty of sparking blaze that became deadly Palisades Fire
data.description:
(KTLA) – A federal jury on Friday convicted a former Uber driver on arson charges for deliberately starting a brush fire that smoldered before eventually exploding into the most destructive wildfire in Los Angeles history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, was found guilty of destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting property used in interstate commerce.

Jurors in Los Angeles deliberated for about two and a half hours before reaching a verdict.

Prosecutors said Rinderknecht used a lighter to ignite the Lachman Fire in the Santa Monica Mountains near Pacific Palisades on Jan. 1, 2025. After fire crews responded and believed they had extinguished the fire, it continued to burn underground for days and reignited as the deadly Palisades Fire.

The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.

Rinderknecht was arrested in Florida nine months later.

Prosecutors argued the former Uber driver was frustrated with his place in society and harbored anger toward wealthy people.

Shortly after midnight on New Year’s Eve, after dropping off a passenger in Pacific Palisades, prosecutors said he walked up a trail, took videos from a nearby hilltop area and listened to music, with the video showing objects being lit on fire.

The conviction comes after a jury was unable to reach a verdict in Rinderknecht’s first trial in June. In that trial, the jury deadlocked 10-2 in favor of acquittal.

Prosecutors also dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.

During the second trial, prosecutors focused on evidence placing Rinderknecht at the fire’s origin and established that he was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.

“He was mad at everything, and frustrated,” said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.

Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times after the Lachman Fire began as he walked down the hill, according to evidence presented at the trial.

Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: “Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?”

These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.

The Palisades Fire began in the Santa Monica Mountains of Los Angeles County on Jan. 7, 2025, and grew to destroy large areas of Pacific Palisades, Topanga, and Malibu before it was fully contained on Jan. 31. Twelve people were killed and 6,837 structures were destroyed.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

data.title: Sotomayor suggests Supreme Court colleagues may applaud midterm results as safeguard
data.description:
Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor on Friday suggested her colleagues may view Democrats’ sweeping victories in the midterm elections as a sign that their recent immunity decision has not eliminated checks on the president.

Speaking in Philadelphia, the liberal justice replied “absolutely” when asked if her colleagues were counting on elections as an institutional safeguard when issuing their landmark ruling granting Trump and former presidents broad criminal immunity.

“My colleagues today would probably applaud the last election, because they believe that if the people don’t like what’s happening, they can speak with their vote. And they did speak,” Sotomayor said.

“Now, they may not have liked the message — but I don’t know that,” she continued, “but what I do know is that they really did believe that, structurally, those things are what protect us against excesses in executive power.”

Sotomayor has continued to publicly rail against the 6-3 decision that granted Trump and former presidents presumptive criminal immunity for their official acts, recently saying she hopes the decision will ultimately be overturned.

On Friday, speaking at an American Philosophical Society event, Sotomayor again condemned the decision and said she doesn’t believe the remaining institutional controls in the political system are enough.

 “I think what they missed was the concept that there was no man in this country — and I use the male version, because that’s the saying — that no man was above the law here,” she said of her colleagues. “I think [that] was always something that was an important part of the calculus in which executives made their decision.”

Sotomayor notably didn’t shut down talk of Supreme Court term limits when asked by an audience member during the 45-minute discussion, though she said it was up to elected officials to decide. The justice noted other countries that don’t have judicial lifetime appointments.

“They either have age limits or they have term limits,” Sotomayor said. “So, they have not needed it to keep um politics out of influencing their judges in the way our founders worried. So, that’s something that should give you pause.”

data.title: Court formally approves $7.25B class settlement for cancer claims from Roundup weed killer
data.description:
A judge Friday formally approved a proposed $7.25 billion agreement to settle current and future cancer claims related to exposure of Monsanto’s Roundup weed killer.

The decision, by Missouri Judge Timothy Boyer, wraps up years of litigation in which people alleged that their exposure to Roundup caused them to develop blood cancers known as non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

The judge described the settlement as being “among the largest in history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements.”

Monsanto and the plaintiffs suing it reached the settlement agreement in February and received preliminary approval in March.

After the agreement and preliminary approval, the Supreme Court made it more difficult for some similar cases to be heard in the future. It particularly ruled that people cannot sue pesticide companies for failing to warn of health impacts not formally recognized by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

The EPA has not linked glyphosate, a key ingredient in Roundup, to health impacts like cancer. In 2015, the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer described it as “probably carcinogenic” to humans.

Boyer cited the Supreme Court’s decision in his final approval of the settlement agreement, saying that even without it, Monsanto has won a majority of related cases.

Christopher A. Seeger, a court-appointed lawyer for one of the subclasses in the case, praised the decision as helping people who were exposed to the weed killer.

“Today’s final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice,” Seeger wrote in a statement. 

Meanwhile, Bill Anderson, the CEO of Bayer, which owns Monsanto, described the approval as “a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” in a written statement. 

Pesticide issues, including those related to glyphosate, have also become a major cause of the Make America Healthy Again movement linked to Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The Trump administration backed Monsanto at the Supreme Court.

data.title: Casten, Lieu propose whistleblower program for prediction market insider trading
data.description:
Reps. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) and Ted Lieu (D-Calif.) introduced new legislation Friday to regulate prediction markets and prevent insider trading, allowing whistleblowers to come forward and report wrongdoing.

The Policing Insider Trading in Prediction Markets Act would create a program at the Justice Department for people with knowledge of insider trading to come forward and potentially receive financial compensation for information leading to successful enforcement.

“Prediction markets have a serious insider trading problem,” Casten said. “By encouraging whistleblowers to come forward and report wrongdoing, we can take an important step in cracking down on insider trading to restore accountability and public confidence in the U.S. rule of law.”

Improper use of betting markets has been in the spotlight multiple times this year, among political candidates, servicemembers and even White House staff.

In August, President Trump’s teleprompter operator was placed on leave and investigated for placing bets on the content of the president’s speeches before they were made public. Later that month, a Republican congressional candidate in North Carolina was suspended from Kalshi for betting on her own race. Kalshi had previously suspended three other congressional candidates in April.

Other examples of misuse include a U.S. Army soldier betting on the U.S. operation in Venezuela and nine accounts on Polymarket making $2.4 million on bets about military action in Iran. House Oversight Committee chair Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) announced an investigation into Kalshi and Polymarket in May.

In a statement about the bill Friday, Lieu cited some of the examples as a reason for legislative action.

“Government insiders should not be able to profit from betting on U.S. military operations or the contents of a President’s speech. They should not be able to use their positions of public trust to manipulate prediction markets,” Lieu said.

Kalshi recently said it had eliminated the option to place bets on Trump’s comments in response to a Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) order, having previously argued that Trump-mention markets “present a heightened risk of manipulation.”

With Republicans still in the majority, Casten and Lieu’s bill will need bipartisan support to pass before the end of the year, though it could be reintroduced once the new Congress — with a sizable Democratic majority — is sworn in.
